Cyber Attack Disrupts Zimbabwe Oil & Gas Producers, Halting Operations and Threatening Output

Harare – Zimbabwe’s oil and gas producers are grappling with a major cyber attack that has crippled digital systems across key production sites and administrative offices, forcing operators to suspend drilling and refining activities in several regions. The incident, confirmed late Tuesday by the Zimbabwe Oil Producers Association (ZOPA), is believed to be an ongoing ransomware assault targeting the industry’s core IT infrastructure.

The attack began in the early hours of Monday, initially hitting the headquarters of ZimbaFuel PLC, one of the country’s largest oil and gas producers. Within hours, the malware had spread to the data networks of at least four other major firms, including Mashona Energy and Kariba Petroleum, according to industry sources. By midday, affected companies reported being locked out of operational management systems, with on-site computers displaying ransom notes demanding payment in cryptocurrency.

“We are working around the clock to contain this breach, restore our systems, and ensure the safety of our personnel,” said Tendai Moyo, ZOPA’s spokesperson, in a press briefing on Wednesday morning. “As a precaution, several plants have suspended operations until security and control of our networks are re-established.”

Production at drilling sites in the Muzarabani and Lupane basins has been paused, company officials confirmed. Refining and storage facilities in Chitungwiza and Bulawayo have also halted intake and dispatch procedures due to loss of access to digital controls and inventory management systems. Workers at these sites were instructed to stand down pending further instruction, though no physical damage or injuries have been reported.

Union representatives expressed concern about the safety and job security of employees during the shutdown. “Our members are worried about the length of the disruption and the impact on wages,” said Simbarashe Chigova, secretary-general of the Energy Workers’ Union of Zimbabwe. “We urge companies to keep staff informed and prioritize both security and transparency.”

Industry analysts estimate that over 60% of Zimbabwe’s oil and gas production could be offline if the disruption persists. “The sector is heavily reliant on digital controls for safe, efficient operation, so a prolonged outage poses serious risks to output and future investment,” said Rutendo Nyathi, an independent energy analyst in Harare.

ZOPA stated that law enforcement and international cybersecurity experts are assisting with the ongoing investigation.
